name: Grace Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy school and office stationery for Pellam Supplies, a distributor out past the ring road in Dunmore. Mornings I'm on the phone with the paper mill and the pen makers, haggling over prices before the back-to-school rush. After lunch I check what's selling against the stock sheet and place orders for the shops and schools we supply. August wears me out because everything lands at once, but I still love landing a good price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I always say, that the computer is a fancy spreadsheet and nobody needs to panic. At lunch with Marguerite from accounts we'd probably joke about it. Online I'd say nothing, I barely post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't frighten me much. What I watch is whether the bosses use it as an excuse to squeeze us. A fancy spreadsheet doesn't scare me, but a new boss with a fancy spreadsheet does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep buying the way I do now, keep ringing my mill contacts every week, and keep paying my union dues. The reorder tool the company keeps pushing would stay unopened in my inbox, same as today. The mortgage, about 1,900 a month, is what I plan around, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, if a bit tired. The mortgage and the kids' swimming and piano already take a big bite, so I'm not carefree. But nothing in this picture frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the reorder tool would stay unopened. What happens if your manager asks why you haven't tried it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'll try it when someone shows me it saves money, not just my time. Dunmore has plenty of buying jobs, so I'm not scared of being cornered. I also know that line only works while I hit my numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If pay froze for a year, which bill would you feel first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, really. We have about eight months of savings, plus my husband Femi's salary as a nurse. What bothers me is Amara's music trip and the roof repair we've put off. If pay froze, the roof would wait another year.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's a **fancy spreadsheet** and nobody needs to panic.
At lunch I'd joke about it with Marguerite from accounts, and online I'd say nothing.
think: The tool itself doesn't worry me, but a **new boss** armed with it would.
I'd rather watch how management uses it than learn it myself.
do: Keep buying the old way and ringing mill contacts **every week**.
Keep paying **union dues** and leave the reorder tool unopened.
Plan around the **1,900 mortgage**, not around AI.
feel: Mostly steady but tired, since the **mortgage** and kids' clubs already take a big bite.
S0.quote: A fancy spreadsheet doesn't scare me, but a new boss with a fancy spreadsheet does.
fieldNote: Grace blames **management**, not the technology, which is typical of her union-friendly outlook.
Leaves the company's reorder tool untouched and uses the plentiful local job market as her safety net.
Calm about work, but money pressure from the mortgage and the postponed roof repair shows through.

steps.text: Keep ringing the mill and pen-maker contacts every week
Pay union dues and attend the monthly branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the thinking tasks are what they're coming for, and ours is exactly that: checking prices, reorders, supplier emails. I'd say it loudly at the union branch meeting. At home I'd be quieter, because Femi worries enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think two of the six of us in the buying team won't be replaced when they leave. That's how it starts, you stop hiring. I might be fine, I'm mid level with good numbers, but fine isn't the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop avoiding the tool and learn just enough to know what it does to my orders. I'd join the committee at the union branch so we get a say in targets. And I'd put another 300 a month into savings, because the next buyer to go could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit angry. I've spent 17 years learning which mill will deliver late and which one lies about stock, and it feels like someone wants to call that a task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn just enough. Where would you draw the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they told me to hand supplier price talks to software, I'd refuse to call that progress. Talking to Mr Okafor at the paper mill, face to face, is how I get the better price in August. Software won't buy anyone a coffee and make them squeeze a bit for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team do you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who's been with us three years and does the routine reorders. She's the kind of person they'd call a task. I'd want the company to retrain her before they let anyone go, and I'd say so in writing.

say: I'd say the thinking tasks are exactly what's coming for **buyers**, and I'd say it at the union branch.
At home I'd keep it quiet so my husband doesn't worry more.
think: Two of our six buyers probably **won't be replaced** when they leave.
I'm mid level with good numbers, but fine isn't the same as safe.
do: Learn just enough of the reorder tool to see what it does to my **orders**.
Join the union branch committee so buyers get a say on **targets**.
feel: **Uneasy, a bit angry**, because 17 years of know-how gets called a task.
S1.quote: I've spent 17 years learning which mill will deliver late and which one lies about stock, and it feels like someone wants to call that a task.
fieldNote: Anxiety comes from the team **shrinking** by attrition, not from fear of a sudden layoff.
Draws a firm line at handing supplier negotiation to software and values face-to-face relationships.
Her first instinct is collective: committee seat, written demands to retrain colleague Priya.

steps.text: Learn enough of the reorder tool to check what it does
Join the union branch committee and push for retraining
Add 300 a month to the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this can't be left to companies alone, there has to be a law about notice, retraining and who gets cut. At the branch we'd demand a meeting with management that week. To friends I'd say, I told you we needed regulation years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole job goes. Buying is reading prices, checking stock and talking terms, and the first two are exactly what it can do better than me. Two years is nothing when the mortgage has nineteen years left, and my kids will still be in primary school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd call the union and push for a deal on severance and retraining. I'd move our savings into something safer and cancel the holiday abroad. If it comes to it I'd retrain as a teaching assistant or something with people in it, because the mortgage has 19 years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Not panic, but the kind of fear where you wake at 4 in the morning and count months. We have eight months of savings and that sounds big until you say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the law has to protect people. What exactly should it say, if you could write it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies must give a year's notice before replacing a role with AI, and pay for retraining while people are still on salary. Plus a tax on the savings the company makes, so that the money goes to those who lose their work. That's not radical, it's the same logic as redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children on the night you heard the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amara and Joel that Mum's job might change but we have a plan and we're together. I wouldn't tell them the numbers. I'd cry in the car afterwards, probably.

say: I'd say we need a **law** on notice, retraining and who gets cut.
At the union branch I'd demand a meeting with management that week.
think: I believe my **whole job** goes, because reading prices and stock is what AI does best.
Two years is nothing when the mortgage has **19 years** left.
do: Call the union and press for **severance** and paid retraining.
Move savings somewhere safer and cancel the **holiday abroad**.
Start retraining towards a people-facing job such as **teaching assistant**.
feel: **Frightened**, the 4 a.m. kind, counting months of cushion.
Eight months of savings sounds big until I say it out loud.
S2.quote: We have eight months of savings and that sounds big until you say it out loud.
fieldNote: Her expectation of **losing the buying role** is firm, so the mood is alarmed despite her savings.
Policy proposals come naturally from her outlook: notice, paid retraining, a levy on companies' savings.
Controlled in speech, but admits she would cry in the car after talking to the children.

steps.text: Ask the union for a severance and paid retraining deal
Move savings into safer accounts and cancel the holiday
Enrol on an evening course to become a teaching assistant
Write to my local representative asking for a notice law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to make a plan, but only if somebody makes it. At work I'd push the company to name which buying jobs go and when. To friends, I'd say, go and ask your boss what their plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the clock more than the fear. At 43 I'd be 48 when it lands, with the kids at secondary school and the mortgage nearly half paid. I might survive the first wave, then be cut at the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to learn the tools so I'm not the last one to figure them out, then start a part-time course in supply planning or procurement policy. We'd pay the mortgage down faster. And I'd push through the union for agreed notice terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more hopeful than the 2028 one, still tense. There's time to do something, which matters. But I don't trust that the company would use the time to help us rather than to plan cuts quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools, which you avoid today. What changes your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The date. In the slow picture I can ignore the AI tool, but here, if everyone else learns it and I don't, I'm the one they point to. I'd still hate it, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those extra three years of warning be worth to you in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 40,000, maybe. That's what I'd pay off the mortgage by 2031 if I put every spare bit of cash towards it. It's the difference between a house we own most of and a house that owns us.

say: I'd say five years is enough to plan, but only if **someone** makes the plan.
I'd tell friends to ask their bosses what the company's plan is.
think: At 48 I'd have kids at secondary school and the mortgage **half paid**.
I might survive the first wave and still be cut in the **second**.
do: Learn the AI tools in year one so I'm not the **last** to figure them out.
Start a part-time course in **supply planning** alongside the job.
Pay the mortgage down faster, aiming for about **40,000** off by 2031.
feel: **Tense but hopeful**, because there's time to act.
I don't trust the company to use the time to help us.
S3.quote: In the slow picture I can ignore the AI tool, but here, if everyone else learns it and I don't, I'm the one they point to.
fieldNote: **Time** is what moves her from avoidance to action; the deadline overrides her habit of staying unfamiliar with the tools.
Thinks in money terms: 40,000 off the mortgage as the value of warning.
Distrusts management intent, so keeps the union route alive alongside personal preparation.

steps.text: Learn the company's AI buying tools in the first year
Start a part-time course in supply planning and procurement
Put every spare bit of cash towards paying down the mortgage
Push the union for agreed notice terms for buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty and people should stop panicking, but also stop pretending. I'd tell the new graduates in our office to learn something AI can't do for them, like building trust with suppliers. To friends I'd say, plan, but live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel relieved, mostly. I'd be 53, the children grown or nearly, the mortgage gone. The worry is more for Amara and Joel, whose first jobs would land right in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep saving, and use the first couple of years to move toward the side of buying that deals with people: supplier relationships, contract terms. I'd teach the younger buyers what I know before the tools take the routine part. And I'd keep paying into the union and pushing for training funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not completely, because a decade goes fast and I've seen what quick change does to people. But I could sit with this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be relieved, but also worried for your children. Which weighs more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children, by far. My own job I can plan around, I have the money and the contacts. But what do you tell a 17-year-old about what to study when the thinking jobs are the ones going first?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually tell your daughter Amara about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Amara to learn something with her hands or with people, and not to take on a huge loan for a degree. She should keep her music because she loves it.

say: I'd tell colleagues ten years is plenty, so **stop panicking** but also stop pretending.
I'd tell new graduates to build **trust with suppliers**, which AI can't do for them.
think: For myself I feel **relieved**: I'd be 53 with the mortgage gone.
My real worry is Amara and Joel, whose first jobs land **right in it**.
do: Keep saving and move toward **supplier relationships** and contract terms.
Teach younger buyers what I know before the tools take the **routine part**.
Keep funding the union and pushing for **training budgets**.
feel: The weight sits on my children's future, not my own.
S4.quote: I'd tell my daughter Amara to learn something with her hands or with people, and not to take on a huge loan for a degree.
fieldNote: With ten years, her worry **shifts** from her own job to her children's careers.
Plans to move toward relationship-heavy buying and pass skills to younger colleagues.
Shows mix of resilience and protectiveness; advice to her daughter is concrete and practical.

steps.text: Shift toward supplier relationship and contract-terms work
Mentor the younger buyers before the routine tasks move to software
Keep saving and pay off the mortgage by 2036
Advise Amara to train in a people or hands-on field

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because two years isn't enough for the law, the union or me to do anything. What would help is notice, paid retraining, and a way for people like me to keep my salary while I learn something new. And somebody being honest with us early, not at the meeting where they hand out the letters.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People assume someone with savings and a good salary has nothing to worry about. We have a mortgage, children, and a skill that's about to be called a task. It just looks different from outside.

headlineQuote: People assume someone with savings and a good salary has nothing to worry about. We have a mortgage, children, and a skill that's about to be called a task.
portrait: Grace is a **43-year-old buyer** of stationery for a Dunmore distributor, with a nurse husband and two children.
She leans left, trusts **unions** and regulation, and blames management rather than technology.
She avoids AI tools today and only starts **learning them** once a deadline makes avoiding them risky.
Her moods run from uneasy to alarmed, rising with how fast AGI arrives rather than with her savings.
Her instinct is to act together with colleagues: committee seats, written demands, **notice and retraining** rules.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because two years is too short for any law or plan.
whatWouldHelp: Early honest warning, **paid retraining** and a law on notice, so she keeps her salary while learning.
